Although people have a desk location they spend between 50% and 70% of their time elsewhere, meaning workstation location does not necessarily provide a good description of how spatial patterns make a person available to others.
Previous work using these methods was carried out in scientific research laboratories with different working practices and cultures, making direct comparison to Company Y uncertain.
Spatial integration alone may be insufficient to support flexible working; spatial differentiation is necessary to provide a range of environments for different work activities.
A higher degree of spatial differentiation in open-plan areas might lead to the emergence of more fixed statuses arguing for privileged rights to space.
The removal of individual rights to space (as in 'romping') could lead to the emergence of 'hidden' power structures.
An apparent 'freeing up' of access to spatial differentiation for all staff may entail a reciprocal 'tightening up' of codes of behaviour and especially those governing space use.
It remains to be seen what form elaborated rule systems will take in company Y to manage nomadic office society and maintain identity.
minimum_safe_summary: This paper presents findings from two empirical case studies (Company X and Company Y) investigating the relationship between office spatial configuration and social interaction, communication, and perceived usefulness among staff. Using space syntax analysis, observations, and questionnaire surveys, the studies found that higher spatial integration and accessibility within a building or specific zones correlated with increased movement, higher frequency of encounters, and a greater number of observed talking people. Crucially, the frequency of being seen by colleagues was strongly associated with being perceived as "useful" in one's work, particularly for staff without direct programmatic work relationships. The paper highlights that while spatial integration can foster unplanned interactions critical for innovation, excessive homogenization of space or segregation (e.g., by silver screen walls) can disrupt these generative interfaces and potentially inhibit local group identity or spontaneous communication. Limitations include the inability to directly link spatial effects to innovation levels in Company X and the challenge of accurately assessing individual availability given staff mobility, as well as the potential for new power structures or behavioral rules to emerge with increased spatial flexibility.
